passage: While researching the migration patterns of loggerhead sea turtles across the western _______ that a significant proportion of juveniles were bypassing traditional nesting beaches in favor of previously unused stretches of coastline along the Sardinian peninsula.

options.text: Mediterranean, marine biologist Dr. Anselmo Ferreira observed
Mediterranean; marine biologist Dr. Anselmo Ferreira observed
Mediterranean marine biologist Dr. Anselmo Ferreira observed
Mediterranean: marine biologist Dr. Anselmo Ferreira observed

explanation: The sentence begins with the dependent clause "While researching the migration patterns of loggerhead sea turtles across the western Mediterranean," which must be followed by a comma before the main clause. The comma after "Mediterranean" correctly separates the introductory dependent clause from the independent clause that follows. The semicolon option is incorrect because a semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides, and the "While" clause is dependent. The option without any punctuation creates a garden-path misreading in which "Mediterranean" appears to modify "marine biologist." The colon option is incorrect because a colon requires a complete independent clause before it, and the "While" clause is not independent.

passage: In a 2022 survey of freshwater biodiversity in the Dinaric Alps, herpetologist Jovan Petrić documented an unexpected _______ over sixty-three percent of the olm salamanders in sampled caves exhibited signs of a chytrid fungal infection that had never before been recorded in the species.

options.text: finding, over
finding: over
finding over
finding; and over

explanation: The sentence structure calls for a colon after "finding" because the preceding clause—"herpetologist Jovan Petrić documented an unexpected finding"—is a complete independent clause, and the material that follows specifies what the finding was. A colon correctly signals that an explanation or elaboration of the finding follows. The comma option creates a comma splice, improperly joining two independent clauses with only a comma. The option with no punctuation produces a run-on sentence, fusing two independent clauses without any separation. The semicolon-plus-conjunction option uses the non-standard combination "; and," which is reserved for separating items in complex lists with internal commas and is not appropriate for joining two independent clauses in this context.

options.text: twenty-nine—historically the cohort least likely to vote in local elections—
twenty-nine, historically the cohort least likely to vote in local elections—
twenty-nine; historically the cohort least likely to vote in local elections,
twenty-nine historically the cohort least likely to vote in local elections,

explanation: The phrase "historically the cohort least likely to vote in local elections" is a nonessential parenthetical appositive describing "residents aged eighteen to twenty-nine." It interrupts the main clause and must be set off by matching punctuation on both sides. The em-dash pair correctly encloses the parenthetical. The option beginning with a comma and ending with an em dash uses mismatched delimiters—a parenthetical interruption must open and close with the same type of punctuation mark. The option using a semicolon to open the parenthetical is incorrect because a semicolon would signal the start of a new independent clause, but "historically the cohort least likely to vote in local elections" is not an independent clause. The option with no opening punctuation and only a trailing comma fails to signal where the parenthetical begins, causing the reader to misparse the sentence structure.

passage: The environmental policy institute published a report examining the effectiveness of carbon pricing mechanisms adopted by seven European nations. The three _______ saw the largest reductions in industrial emissions, with declines averaging twenty-one percent over a six-year period.

options.text: nations that implemented a revenue-neutral carbon tax before 2015
nations, that implemented a revenue-neutral carbon tax before 2015,
nations, which implemented a revenue-neutral carbon tax before 2015,
nations that implemented a revenue-neutral carbon tax before 2015,

explanation: The relative clause "that implemented a revenue-neutral carbon tax before 2015" is restrictive: it identifies which three of the seven nations the sentence is about. A restrictive clause uses "that" without commas, so the option with "that" and no commas is correct. The option pairing "that" with enclosing commas is incorrect because commas signal a nonrestrictive (extra-information) clause, and Standard English does not use "that" to introduce nonrestrictive clauses. The option using ", which" with commas treats the clause as nonrestrictive, implying that all three nations are already identified and the carbon-tax detail is parenthetical—but the clause is essential for specifying which three nations are meant. The option using "that" with a trailing comma but no opening comma creates an asymmetrical construction that incorrectly separates the relative clause from the verb "saw" with a comma, disrupting the connection between the subject and its predicate.

passage: The collection of pressed botanical specimens from the highlands of _______ over two hundred rare fern species, many of which were previously undocumented in the region's ecological surveys.

options.text: Borneo includes
Borneo include
Borneo are including
Borneo have included

explanation: The subject of the sentence is "collection," which is singular and requires a singular verb. The singular form "includes" correctly agrees with "collection." The plural form "include" incorrectly treats the subject as plural, likely reflecting a misidentification of the plural noun "specimens" or "highlands" as the subject. The plural progressive form "are including" makes the same subject-verb agreement error while also introducing an unnecessary progressive aspect. The plural perfect form "have included" again uses a plural verb with the singular subject "collection" and shifts the tense to present perfect without contextual justification.

passage: When the archaeologist first examined the Lydian tomb complex in 2019, she noted that the foundation stones _______ significant weathering. In her most recent assessment, conducted last month, she observed that erosion has continued to degrade the structural integrity of the remaining walls.

options.text: had undergone
have undergone
undergo
would undergo

explanation: The past perfect form "had undergone" is required here because the weathering of the foundation stones occurred before the archaeologist's 2019 examination—an event that is itself already in the past. The past perfect correctly establishes this sequence of two past events. The present perfect form "have undergone" incorrectly situates the weathering as extending to the present moment, conflicting with the past-tense narrative frame established by "first examined" and "she noted." The simple present form "undergo" is inconsistent with the past-tense context of the 2019 examination. The conditional form "would undergo" implies a hypothetical or future-in-the-past scenario, but the weathering had already occurred—it was not speculative or anticipated.

passage: The implications of the recent discovery by a team of paleontologists working in the Gobi Desert—that a previously unknown species of tyrannosaur roamed the region roughly sixty-eight million years ago—_______ still being debated by researchers who study Late Cretaceous ecosystems.

options.text: are
is
has been
was

explanation: The subject of the sentence is "implications," a plural noun that requires the plural verb "are." The long dash-enclosed parenthetical—"that a previously unknown species of tyrannosaur roamed the region roughly sixty-eight million years ago"—and the intervening prepositional phrases ("of the recent discovery," "by a team of paleontologists") create substantial distance between the subject and its verb, tempting the reader to match the verb with a nearer singular noun such as "discovery," "team," or "species." The singular form "is" fails to agree with the plural subject "implications." The singular present-perfect form "has been" likewise does not agree with the plural subject. The singular past-tense form "was" both fails in agreement and incorrectly shifts the debate into the past, whereas the sentence indicates the debate is ongoing.

passage: _______ the seventeenth-century shipwreck contained remarkably well-preserved navigational instruments, including a brass astrolabe and two ivory compasses.

options.text: Surveying the seafloor off the coast of Mozambique, marine archaeologist Dr. Yuki Tanabe's preliminary report confirmed that
Surveying the seafloor off the coast of Mozambique, marine archaeologist Dr. Yuki Tanabe confirmed that
Having been surveyed off the coast of Mozambique, marine archaeologist Dr. Yuki Tanabe confirmed that the seafloor near
Having surveyed the seafloor off the coast of Mozambique, it was confirmed by marine archaeologist Dr. Yuki Tanabe that

explanation: The participial phrase "Surveying the seafloor off the coast of Mozambique" must modify the subject of the main clause that follows. In the correct option, the subject is "marine archaeologist Dr. Yuki Tanabe"—a person who can logically perform the action of surveying. The option whose main-clause subject is "preliminary report" creates a dangling modifier: a report cannot survey the seafloor. The option beginning with "Having been surveyed" produces a dangling modifier in which "marine archaeologist Dr. Yuki Tanabe" appears to have been surveyed, rather than having conducted a survey—the passive voice misattributes the action. The option beginning with "Having surveyed" pairs the participial phrase with the pronoun "it," an expletive that cannot perform the action of surveying; this construction creates both a dangling modifier and an unnecessarily convoluted passive sentence.
